**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Say where your question
came from, who would act on the answer or pay for it, and which of seven shapes
it takes. Map what it needs against what your team has, name the row that binds and
the date it has to close by, and say what the question becomes if it does not.

::: {.callout-note title="What to take away" appearance="simple"}
What makes an answer valuable. **Public value** is shared, so nobody can be stopped from using the answer and it gets published. **Private value** can be kept, so somebody pays for it. Both are fine here. The test is not whether one person acts, it is whether you can keep the answer.

Ideas arrive by three routes. From the world, from a study, and from data. Route one lacks data, route two lacks novelty, route three lacks a decision.

Four questions kill most bad ideas. Can three to five people do it in a semester? Can you name the data, who holds it, and how you get it? Could the answer come out either way? Would anybody act differently?

The resource map is six rows against what the question needs: data, comparison, skills, time and money, permissions, people and access. A resource that turns out missing changes the question, and every redraw is the plan working.
:::

## Due today

Your team's question sheet and the resource map of the question that survives.
Both before you leave.

# 1. What makes a good idea

## What makes a good idea

- You need a way to quickly evaluate ideas, otherwise you hang on to less interesting ideas for too long.
- An good idea has to check a few boxes:

1. Importance. Somebody is better off knowing the answer.
2. Feasible. One can actually get the answer with existing data and methods.
3. Novelty. The answer is not already known.
4. Fit. The idea is great for your team. You have the skills and comparative advantage to tackle it.

- You can rank ideas based on these criteria to pick ideas with high potential for your team.

::: {.notes}
One and a half minutes. Put the four up and do not explain them yet. One
slide each follows.

Say why this comes first. You already have ideas, so the useful thing is
not another way to generate them. It is a way to sort them fast. The cost
of having no test is not that you pick a bad idea on purpose. It is that
you stay with a mediocre one for weeks because nothing told you to drop it.

Say that the four are not weighted equally in this course. Feasible is the
one that kills projects in March, so it gets the whole second half of the
hour.

Say also that they pull against each other. The most important questions are
usually the least feasible, and the most feasible are usually the least new.
A project is a choice about where to sit between them, not a search for a
question that scores full marks on all four.

The fourth is the one they will not expect and it is the one that stops a
team adopting somebody else's good idea. Flag it here and let the fourth
slide do the work.
:::

## What makes a question important

- Answering the question provide value to someone.
- The value you bring can be a private or a public good.
- Private good: e.g. you shed light on an untapped market segment for a company (value is derived by acting upon the private information, not publishing it)
- Public good: e.g. you shed light on how changing a policy could improve economic surplus (value is derived by publishing)
- In academia, the important is often measure by how many other academics find the work useful (determines journals and drives citations)
- Key idea: someone is better off after we responded to this question.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is the test that the last two cohorts failed, and it is
the one the room will resist, because a big topic feels important.

Push on the difference. Climate change is large. Whether a flood changes what
a lender charges is important, because somebody acts on the answer.

Do not resolve who acts and who pays here. That is the next block, and it is
where this test gets its second half.
:::

## What makes an answer valuable

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- Somebody or some organization has a decision to make that would benefit from it, or a whole agenda cannot move without it.
- If you cannot identify the people or organizations benefiting from the new knowledge, then it's unclear this is important.
- **Public good value** is shared: many people are better off and you cannot stop anyone using the answer, so it is hard to charge for and it gets published.
- **Private good value** can be kept: one person's decision changes, and that person can keep the answer to themselves, so somebody pays for it.
- Both are fine for this project. Private value has greater traction in private industry.

:::

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. This is the fourth filter, would anybody act
differently, arriving early. Say the word value and leave the slide up.

The bullet that says the test is whether the answer can be kept is what
makes quiz item 1 work, because a student who learned "private means
somebody acts" picks the wrong distractor without it.

Neither definition uses the word excludable. Say "you cannot stop anyone
using it" out loud too, because the term is not what is being examined.

The theory behind the public half is [Arrow
1962](https://www.nber.org/chapters/c2144) on knowledge as a
non-excludable good, cited on the companion page and not on the slide.

Say plainly that the grade does not prefer private.
:::

An investment fund would pay for this while it is the only one holding

:::

Finance ministries and the World Bank act on a published number. Insurers
would pay for the same number, because it is what they price the cover

## What makes a question feasible

- You can get the data, in the time you have, with the skills on the team.
- Feasibility is about resources. It is not about whether the question could be answered by somebody.
- Most projects fail here, so it is critical to evaluate this as early as possible.
- A check: can you pin point the data you are using (if using secondary data) or have an idea of the platform to run your experiments (if working with primary data).

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Say plainly that this is the one that does the killing, and
that it is why the second half of the hour is one long exercise in it.

Checked, not assumed, is the phrase to repeat. It comes back on the map as
the difference between a have and a need.

The whole resource map is this test taken seriously, so this slide is its
promise. Do not open the map here.
:::

## What makes a question novel

- Nobody has already answered it, and you know that because you went and looked.
- Requires that you read and look around extensively.
- New does not mean nobody has worked on the topic (that could be a sign this is not important). Instead, it means this answer is not already out there (e.g. a publication, a product or service line, etc.).
- A marginal change to published work is new, but not as important (you need to recognize this).
- The check: what is the closest study to ours, and clearly identify how your study sheds light on something the previous study did not provide any insight.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is the test that sends them to the literature, and it is
the only reason this course asks them to read.

Tie it back to the second route without naming a team. A marginal change
passes this test at the low end, and that is acceptable for one semester as
long as the team knows where it is sitting.

The honest failure here is not being unoriginal. It is not having looked.
:::

## Private value disappears once it is published

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- [McLean and Pontiff](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) collected 97 published rules for picking stocks that beat the market.
- On average a rule earned 26 percent less on later data than in the study that found it, and 58 percent less once it was in print.
- A rule is worth money while one trading desk is the only one using it, and about half that once it is in a journal.
- A search-traffic signal regressed on next-day returns has no trading desk and no journal, so it has neither kind of value.
- If an answer is worth money and nobody has produced it, ask why, and read to check that nobody has.
- A public good does not lose its value like this.
:::

[McLean and Pontiff (2016), *Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?*, Journal of Finance 71(1), 5 to 32](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is why signal-on-returns is a fine desk memo and a
bad capstone.

Nobody in the room has to have read a finance paper. Return predictor is
"a rule for picking stocks that beat the market", out of sample is "on
later data", and both are said that way on the slide.

The figures and the DOI are verified, so they go on the slide as numbers
and not as "about". Do not say "near zero": it was wrong and contradicted
the paper cited one bullet above it.

The last bullet is meeting 1's line on what reading is for, turned into a
reason to go to the literature.
:::

## What makes a question a good fit for you

- A question can be important, feasible and new, and still not be a good fit.
- Fit is two things: the skills your team actually has, and whether you care about it.
- A question nobody on the team can execute is somebody else's project, however good it is.
- The check: do we know the skills we have in the team? Do we have the excitement and commitment for this? Are we well organized and know who does what?

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is the instructor's own fourth test and it is the one
that is missing from every version of this advice they will read elsewhere.

Say the failure case plainly. A team adopts a question because it sounds
important, nobody on it can do the hardest part, and by February the project
is being done badly by the one person who can.

Interest is not softness. The question that gets finished is the one somebody
still wants to answer when it has stopped being fun, and that is a
feasibility fact rather than a preference.

This is also the argument for the inventory on "Start from what you have",
forty minutes from now. Do not open it here, just plant it.
:::

# 2. Types of ideas

## A project can take different shapes

::: {style="font-size:0.56em"}

| | The question it asks | For example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 Evaluation | Did it work? Somebody changed something and you measure what it did | Did the loyalty card raise what people spend? |
| 2 Preference and pricing | What would people choose and pay? Nobody has decided yet, so you ask them | Would shoppers pay more for a lower carbon label? |
| 3 Prediction and risk | What happens next? You need the number, not the reason | Which customers will cancel next quarter? |
| 4 Diagnosis | Why is this so uneven? Something varies and nobody knows why | Why do some stores sell twice what similar stores do? |
| 5 Feasibility | Is this opportunity real, and what is in the way? | Is there a market for this product in Kenya? |
| 6 Measurement | How much of this is there? Nobody has counted it, so you build the number | What does one flood actually cost a county? |
| 7 Valuation | What is this worth? You price it against things that already carry prices | What is a water view worth on a house? |

:::

- The same interest can usually be turned into three of these, so pick the one you can answer.

::: {.notes}
Three and a half minutes. This slide defines the five. The next one kills
them, so do not give away the failures here.

Read the middle column out. It is written for somebody who has never taken
an econometrics course, and the examples are there so nobody has to guess
what the label means.

Rows six and seven were added on 2026-09-09 because five did not cover the
room. Measurement is how much of this is there when nobody has counted it,
and it is where the climate damage question sits. Valuation is what is this
worth, priced against comparable things, and it is where the asset pricing
question sits. Neither team is named on the screen.

The old version of this slide showed only the failure column, which named
five categories it never defined. It was cryptic and it was cut on
2026-09-09.

The can-claim column is spoken rather than shown, and all four columns are
printed on the companion page. Say the one line that matters: one and two
can support a claim about cause, three cannot and must not pretend to, four
is a description that points at a cause somebody could test later, and five
needs at least one piece of the team's own evidence or it is a literature
review.

Then say Team H's sentence as three shapes, as a gift. The sentence is
"does AI advice move a non-expert closer to a good decision, or just swap
their overconfidence for the model's?". Evaluation: did people given AI
advice decide better than people without it? Preference: which advice
format do people choose, and what would they pay for it? Prediction: who
over-relies, and can you tell in advance?

A team that hears its own interest in one of those three has found its
afternoon's first job.
:::

# 3. How you come up with ideas

## Ideas arrive in three ways

1. From the world. Something you noticed, or a decision somebody has to make.
2. From previous work. A marginal change to something already published.
3. From data. A file you can already reach, worked backwards to a question.

- One slide each follows, and each one ends with the thing that route leaves missing.

::: {.notes}
One minute. Put the three up and take them one at a time afterwards.

Say the shape of the block before it starts: the world lacks data, previous
work lacks novelty, data lacks a decision. They will hear each of those
again on its own slide, so do not explain them here.

Meeting 1's page calls the data route "route 5". Say once, and only once,
that the five collapsed into three, because a gap and an extension are both
previous work, and an anomaly and a decision are both the world.
:::

## Getting ideas from the world

- From the world: a problem you saw, and it usually arrives without being sought.
- It comes from the news, from a conversation with a colleague, or from a job you have done yourself.
- The good ones often come out of an unexpected conversation rather than out of sitting down to think.
- You start with the problem and go looking for data afterwards, so data is the row most likely to be empty.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is the route most of the room arrived on.

No team is named on this slide or on the two that follow. Naming one makes
the route a verdict on their question, and the three routes are not a
ranking.

Say once, and only once, that meeting 1's page calls the data route
"route 5", and that the five collapsed into three, because a gap and an
extension are both previous work, and an anomaly and a decision are both
the world.

Gate. This slide is on screen by 2:11. If it is not, run all three route
slides at a minute each by dropping the third bullet from every one.
:::

## Getting ideas from previous work

- From previous work: you take an existing idea, generally published, and change it at the margin.
- The change is usually a new setting, a new period, or a limitation the original authors name themselves.
- Read the limitations section, because that is where the authors write down what they could not do.
- This route tends to be marginal, and saying so is honest rather than modest. For one semester it is the right size.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Marginal is the instructor's own word for this route and it
is not a criticism. Say it plainly.

The data usually exists already, because the first study needed it. What is
missing here is novelty, and novelty is not a row on the map, which is why
the reading has to happen before the data work rather than after it.

Do not say which team in this room is on this route. Several are.
:::

## Getting ideas from data

- From data: you start from a file you can reach and work backwards to a question it could answer.
- Data is usually the binding constraint, so this route makes the constraint visible on day one.
- Expect to go back and forth. You get the file, find what it does not contain, and revise the question.
- That revising is not the plan failing. It is the loop the rest of this hour is about.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. This is the instructor's own account of the route: the data
constrains the question, and the question moves.

Gloss Dewey here, in one clause, because it is named on the access ladder
forty minutes from now and nowhere in between: the data marketplace the
business school subscribes to, free to them, and approval takes days.

The reverse-engineering is the next slide, so do not deliver the warning
here. The fourth bullet is its set-up, and it is also the first statement
of the loop the resource map draws.
:::

## Working backwards from data honestly

- What could this data answer?
- Which of those would anybody act on?
- What does it not contain that you would need?
- You are allowed to walk away from the data.
- Starting from data is the only route where the data is already in hand, so nothing looks missing, and only the question of who would act can kill it.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. The first four lines are meeting 1's, said once and not
re-taught.

The fifth is the new thing and it is why the slide survives. It is the
hook into "What your question needs against what you have",
and it is the tell the shared case turns on after the break.

The map words belong to that slide and not to this one, so do not say
"the data row is full and the gap column is empty" here. Say what the
bullet says.

If the 2:16 gate is missed, the whole slide becomes one spoken sentence
on "Which route did your team's question come from?" and the fifth line
is the sentence.
:::

## Session A · 2:05 to 3:15

The hour has one job. You leave with more candidate questions than you need,
and a reason to kill most of them that you can say out loud. There are two
such reasons: **who would act on the answer or pay for it**, and **what it
would take to get it**. Six blocks build those two reasons, and the last of
them, the resource map, is the one you keep using after today.

### What you drew last week, and the last two cohorts

Last Wednesday your team drew a picture of its own question: what you would
change, and what you would measure. That picture is not yet a question. It
becomes one when you can say what data it needs and who holds that data. So
the hour opens with a question you answer to yourself. Can you name the file
your question needs and the organisation that holds it? Most people
go down, and I do not resolve that on the slide. The hour resolves it. It ends
with one page: what your question needs, what you already have, and what is
missing.

Then thirteen capstone titles from the last two cohorts, and sixty seconds on
the timer to write, on the half sheet on your seat, what most of them have in
common.

From 2026: environmental regulation and ESG strategy on ROE in oil and gas;
inventory turnover in US retail; the VIX on S&P 500 daily returns; Wikipedia
pageviews on stock returns; and what drives engagement with TikTok product
video.

From 2023: Twitter sentiment on NFT returns; social media sentiment on stock
returns; weather on stock returns; ESG score on annual return. Beside those,
organic food choices, Gen Z and sustainable fashion, a digital marketing
strategy, and streaming business models.

**Four of the five 2026 projects were the same project.** Take a public
measure anybody can download. Regress a financial outcome on it. Report a
coefficient. Free data, no design, and nobody named who would act on the
number. 2023 had the same four, and four others about consumer behaviour, and
several of those collected their own data.

I let you find that rather than saying it first, because it lands harder when
you have written it down than when I say it. The same slide comes back twice
today, once at value and once at the shapes.

### Finding the question is the job

Most of your education has rewarded execution. This course rewards the part
before it. In research, having the idea counts as much as being able to
answer it. In business the same skill has a different name: a proposition
that has value. You can only see the value of a new answer against what is
already known, which is what reading is for.

One thing about choosing. The questions people finish are the ones they were
curious about in March. Pick one you would still want to answer when it stops
being fun.

Here is what knowing the literature buys you. Whether generative AI raises
productivity has already been measured, in call centres by
[Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond](https://doi.org/10.3386/w31161) and on writing
tasks by [Noy and Zhang](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586). "Whether"
is taken. The live question is which tasks and for whom, and that is Team A's
sentence: *Does generative AI actually raise the productivity of the people
who use it, and which tasks get the gain?*

### Ideas arrive by three routes, and each leaves something missing

1. **From the world.** A problem you saw, or a decision somebody has to make.
   Team B's sentence is this route: *Do hours, rest, visa status and workplace
   norms change how people perform, or just who takes the job?*
2. **From a study.** A result you would extend, contest or move to a new
   setting. "When a stock suddenly draws a lot of attention, does its price
   rise above what the company's earnings justify, and then fall back?" is a
   follow-up to
   [Da, Engelberg and Gao](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2011.01679.x),
   and it is Team D's sentence.
3. **From data.** A dataset you hold, and a question worked backwards onto
   it. Where do people move after a mass layoff in their county, worked out
   from factory closure notices, which employers have to file before a large
   layoff, sitting next to address histories on Dewey, the data marketplace
   the business school subscribes to. That is lead 5 on the
   [project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd) page.

Route one, from the world, lacks data. Route two, from a study, lacks novelty.
Route three, from data, lacks a decision. So your route tells you where your
gap will be this afternoon.

[Meeting 1](01-introductions.qmd) counted five routes and called the data one
route five. I have collapsed the five into three, because a gap and an
extension are both a study read, and an anomaly and a decision are both the
world.

**Working backwards from data honestly.** What could this
data answer? Which of those would anybody act on? What does it not contain
that you would need? And you are allowed to walk away from the data. Starting
from data is the only route where the data is already in hand, so nothing
looks missing, and only the question of who would act can kill it. That is
also what the shared case after the break turns on.

### What makes an answer valuable

Somebody has a decision waiting on it, or a research area cannot move until it
is answered. Name the person. If you cannot name one, the value is not there
yet.

**Public value** is shared: many people are better off and you cannot stop
anyone using the answer, so it is hard to charge for and it gets published.
That nobody can be stopped from using an idea once it is out, which
economists call non-excludable, is
[Arrow's](https://www.nber.org/chapters/c2144) point about invention, and it
is why public-value work is funded rather than sold.

**Private value** can be kept: one person's decision changes, and that person
can keep the answer to themselves, so somebody pays for it.

The test is not whether one person acts, but whether the answer can be kept
from everybody else. A city transport office is one person deciding, and its
answer is still public value, because the finding gets published and no firm
can hold it.

Both are fine in this course, and the grade does not prefer private. Private
value is easier to sell. Public value is easier to publish.

Try it. Public, private, or both?

| | |
|--:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | When a stock suddenly draws a lot of attention, does its price rise above what the company's earnings justify, and then fall back? |
| 2 | When extreme weather hits a poor country, how much damage does it leave, and is that enough to change decisions? |

<details class="test"><summary>Answers</summary>

One is private. An investment fund would pay for this while it is the only one
holding the answer. Ask instead whether small investors lose money and your
reader is a regulator, which is a different project. Two is both. Finance
ministries and the World Bank act on a published number, and reinsurers would
pay for the same number, because it is what they price the cover on. The label
is the cheap half. The lesson is the third column: who acts, or who pays. A
team that can fill it has answered the question that kills most projects,
would anybody act differently.

</details>

**Private value disappears once it is published.**
[McLean and Pontiff](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) collected 97
published rules for picking stocks that beat the market. On average a rule
earned 26 percent less on later data than in the study that found it, and 58
percent less once it was in print. So a rule is worth money while one trading
desk is the only one using it, and about half that once it is in a journal.
The 2026 Wikipedia pageviews poster had no trading desk and no journal, so it
had neither kind of value. And if an answer is worth money and nobody has
produced it, ask why, and read to check that nobody has.

Write it down while the examples are still up: the role of the person who
would act on your team's answer, and whether they would pay. "Companies" is
not a role. "The head of pricing at a grocery chain" is. If that person is
inside a firm, the firm usually holds the data too, and that is a resource. If
it is the public, the data is usually free and your competition is what is
already published. Keep the half sheet. That line goes on your question sheet
after the break, in the same words.

Value says why. The shape says what you can claim.

### A project can take different shapes

| | Dies when |
|:--|:--|
| 1 Evaluation | there is no credible comparison group |
| 2 Preference and pricing | what people say they would do is reported as what they did |
| 3 Prediction and risk | the team quietly starts recommending what to change |
| 4 Diagnosis and benchmarking | description is dressed up as a cause |
| 5 Feasibility and landscape | it becomes a summary of what other people already found |

The full four-column version, with what each shape asks and what it can
claim, is below.

The same interest can take three shapes, so pick the one you can get the
comparison for, not the one that sounds biggest. Team H's sentence, *Does AI
advice move a non-expert closer to a good decision, or just swap their
overconfidence for the model's?*, is three different projects. As an
evaluation: did people given AI advice decide better than people without it?
As preference and pricing: which advice format do people choose, and what
would they pay for it? As prediction and risk: who over-relies, and can you
tell in advance?

Try it. Which shape is each of these?

| | |
|--:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Did a brand's livestream lift its sales that week? |
| 2 | Can card spending tell you a retailer's sales before the retailer reports them? |

<details class="test"><summary>Answers</summary>

One is evaluation, and it dies without the weeks that brand would have had
without the stream. Two is prediction and risk, and it dies the moment it
tells somebody to buy or sell. Two is the trap: it invites causal talk and
must not get any. Nobody in this room is doing shape five, feasibility and
landscape, and that is right.

</details>

**A date gives you a comparison, and a buyer gives you a decision.** Four of
the five 2026 projects were prediction or diagnosis, and none of them said so.
The repairs are all on questions this room is already asking.

A company's AI claim in a public filing has a date, so there is a before and
an after, and a regulator who reads it. That is Team E's sentence: *Does the
claim show up in revenue and stock price, and does the market only believe
credible firms?*

Team D asks whether a price that rose too far falls back, which is a
prediction that can fail, and saying so is part of the grade.

Team F's sentence, *When a price is set on a company or a pool of assets, do
observable traits explain it, and does it hold?*, asks what a company or a
pool of assets is worth, so it needs the price that would have been set
otherwise, and the next board pricing a deal is the buyer.

The pitch at [meeting 9](09-designs-ii.qmd) asks for the shape by name, and a
project that cannot pick one is not yet a project.

### Six ways a project dies, and four questions that kill most of them

1. The topic with no question.
2. The dataset in search of a question.
3. The consulting deck, which summarises what is already known.
4. The project whose data you cannot get.
5. The dissertation, too big for one spring.
6. The question somebody has already answered.

Four of these six are what a room names before anybody teaches them, and
yours named them on August 26. The dataset in search of a question is starting
from data done any way other than the one honest form above.

Then the filter, which is four questions and is the index of this whole hour.

1. Could a team of three to five execute this in one spring semester?
2. Can you name the dataset, who holds it, and how you get it, checked rather
   than assumed?
3. Could the answer come out either way?
4. Would anybody act differently depending on it?

A no on any one is fatal, and it is cheap to discover today. The either-way
question was last Wednesday. The who-acts question was the value block earlier
today. The other two are the resource map, which is the rest of the afternoon.

Compared to what? Would those two groups have looked the same anyway? Those
two questions are not a fifth filter. They are how "could the answer come out
either way" gets teeth, and they are printed beside the comparison row of the
one page you build next.

This afternoon you write three candidates before you filter one, because a
filter needs a choice. And if two candidates survive all four, take the one
whose worst gap closes soonest, then the one with a named person who acts.
That is the only rule today that discriminates rather than kills, so it goes
on your question sheet too.

The reason to generate first and judge second is arithmetic: one candidate
cannot be filtered. Do not take it as evidence about being judged.
[Diehl and Stroebe](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.53.3.497) found that
most of the loss in group brainstorming comes from taking turns to speak, and
that the fear of being judged contributed little.

### Start from what you have

Sarasvathy's expert entrepreneurs start from who they are, what they know and
whom they know. That is
[effectuation](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2001.4378020). The 2001 paper is
the theory, and the empirical work behind it is a think-aloud study of 27
expert entrepreneurs, so take it as a habit that works and not as a law.

The research version is the same list: the programming languages your team
knows, a dataset you can reach, a person you can email. Somebody who has
worked a warehouse shift knows what the schedule data does not record, and
lived experience of a setting is a resource like any other.

The page that follows sets that list against what the question needs.

**What your question needs against what you have.** The rows are
data, comparison, skills, time and money, permissions, and people and access.
The columns are what the question needs; what you have, and how you checked;
the gap; and who closes it, by when, or how the question moves.

Compared to what? Would those two groups have looked the same anyway? Those
two questions are printed on the sheet beside the comparison row. If you have
not opened the file yourself, write it as a need and not as a have. The last
column is where the plan lives.

Most haves become needs on a first map. That is expected. It is the map
working, not the team failing.

**Access takes minutes or months.**

| You want | How long |
|:--|:--|
| Library databases, FRED, EDGAR, data.census.gov | Now |
| The Nielsen public-use extract, 2019, three product categories | Now, with your netID |
| Dewey | Days |
| Your own survey or online experiment | Weeks, after the IRB, the board that reviews research on people |
| Full Kilts-Nielsen data | Months |
| A data-use agreement with a firm | Months, and it may fail |
| Confidential Census or BLS microdata via FSRDC | Longer than this degree |

Write how long, for every dataset, in the time row and in the permissions row.
The IRB and a data-use agreement are gates. [Meeting 4](04-ethics.qmd) teaches
them, and today you only name which one you trip. The same seven durations, in
the same words, are on the [data sources](../data-sources.qmd) page and at the
foot of the map sheet.

Two cases get built on the screen, and a different row stops each one.

The livestream case is stopped by data. Sales by brand by week exist on
Dewey's Brand Tracker, but a record of who streamed when does not exist
anywhere you can reach. So the question moves. No schedule: move to US brands
whose platform publishes its events. Still nothing: move to one brand with a
public stream log. Still nothing: collect it yourself, which puts money and
the IRB on the map and makes it a job of weeks, and
[meeting 8](08-designs-i.qmd) asks whether that is actually open to you. The
question moved three times and the plan did not fail once.

The nutrition-label case is stopped somewhere else. Nobody holds that data, so
you would build it, and the rows that stop you are money and, more than money,
the clock.

Case one was stopped by a file that does not exist and case two by the
calendar, and nothing but the map tells you which one you are in. The row that
stops you is your **binding row**, and it is the first of the three lines at
the foot of the sheet. Both maps are filled in below.

**The map is redrawn every time a row changes.**

Every move is one line in your decision log: what changed, when, and why. The
map is redrawn three times before the pitch. [Meeting 4](04-ethics.qmd) fills
the permissions row. [Meeting 5](05-tools-and-ai.qmd) checks the data row
against a real file. [Meeting 8](08-designs-i.qmd) asks whether you can build
the comparison row. The pitch at [meeting 9](09-designs-ii.qmd) is the top
line of this map and its data row. A team whose map never moves has not
looked.

### Public value and private value, all seven examples

Two of these reach the screen. All seven are here, because the label is the
easy half and the last column is the part you have to write on your question
sheet.

| Example | Label | Why | Who pays or acts |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| When a stock suddenly draws a lot of attention, does its price rise above what the company's earnings justify, and then fall back? (Team D's sentence) | private | An answer you can trade on is one you can keep to yourself, and it is worth nothing the moment everybody knows it. The public version, whether small investors lose money, is a different question with a regulator as its reader | An investment fund pays while it is the only one holding the answer. [Barber and Odean 2008](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhm079) on buying what is in the news and [Da, Engelberg and Gao 2011](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2011.01679.x) on the fall back answered the first version of it, so the value lies in what they left open, which is what reading checks |
| When extreme weather hits a poor country, how much damage does it leave, and is that enough to change decisions? (Team G's sentence) | both | Governments and aid agencies act on a published number and nobody can be stopped from using it, but the same number prices insurance that pays out automatically once a storm passes a threshold | Finance ministries and the World Bank act; reinsurers would pay to price the cover |
| Does the claim show up in revenue and stock price, and does the market only believe credible firms? (Team E's sentence) | both | Protecting investors is public work and a published answer changes how filings are reviewed; the same answer tells a short seller which firms to bet against | The SEC, the US securities regulator, and auditors act; analysts and short sellers pay |
| Did salary disclosure laws change what employers post? ([lead 9](../project-ideas.qmd)) | public | Every worker in the next state benefits, the answer cannot be kept, and the buyer is a legislature, which does not pay researchers | The next state's legislators act; there is nobody to charge, so it gets published |
| Which store locations sell less than the area they draw customers from should deliver? ([lead 7](../project-ideas.qmd)) | private | One operator acts on it and would never publish the answer, but the data on who lives near each store is bought from a vendor, so what stops you is access to the chain rather than the data | The chain's head of operations pays, or lends its own transaction file in exchange for the answer |
| Does a logo aligned to the drinking spout raise recognition and intent to buy? (the soda-can project, from an earlier cohort) | private | One brand's packaging decision, and the answer is worth nothing to anyone else | A soda company gave them thousands of cans, which is a firm paying in kind for an answer it wanted |
| Does disclosing that a video is AI-generated change how people rate it? ([lead 28](../project-ideas.qmd), a neighbour of Team J) | both | Platforms and brands would pay to know before a disclosure rule lands; the rule itself is public | A platform's head of trust and safety pays; a regulator writing a disclosure rule acts |

### The seven shapes in full

The slide shows each shape, the question it asks and an example. Here are all four columns.

| Shape | Asks | Can claim | Dies when |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 Evaluation | Did it work? A decision was already made somewhere, and you estimate its effect | A causal effect, after the fact, if you can measure the thing you care about before and after, both for the group that got the change and for a credible comparison group | There is no credible comparison group, or the change was taken up precisely by the units that were already moving |
| 2 Preference and pricing | What would people choose, and what would they pay? The decision is not yet made, and what it needs is what people value | A causal effect on what people chose in your task, which is a real limitation and not a footnote | What people say they would do is reported as what they did, or forty classmates are generalised to a market |
| 3 Prediction and risk | What happens next, and how wrong could we be? The decision needs a number about the future, not a cause | How accurately it predicts, tested on later data it has not seen, against an honest baseline, and explicitly not a cause | It is never tested on later data, or the team quietly starts recommending what to change off a model that only predicts |
| 4 Diagnosis and benchmarking | Where is the gap, and what explains it? Something varies more than it should and nobody knows why | Description, plus a theory about why that somebody could later test, honest about being a first step | Description is dressed up as a cause, or the team stops at a dashboard without naming a decision |
| 5 Feasibility and landscape | Is this opportunity real, and what constrains it? | A synthesis of what is known, plus at least one piece of original data the team analyses itself | It becomes a summary of what other people already found, with no evidence of the team's own |
| 6 Measurement | How much of this is there, and how would you know? Nobody has counted it, so the project is building the number | A defensible quantity, and what it shows, provided you say plainly what it counts and what it leaves out | The measure is never checked against anything outside itself, or what it excludes is never stated |
| 7 Valuation | What is this worth? You price the thing against things that already carry prices | A price, provided the things you compare against are genuinely comparable and you say what makes them so | The comparison set is chosen until the answer looks right, or the traits doing the work are not observable to anybody else |

### Case one, the livestream

Does a brand's livestream lift its sales that week? Shape one, evaluation.
Route one, from the world. This one sits very close to something a student in
this room wrote, and I say so rather than pretending otherwise. Nobody is
being asked to defend it. It survives by moving, and the moving is the lesson.
Value: private, because the brand's marketing head decides whether to pay a
host again, and the platform would pay too.

| Row | Need | Have, and how checked | Gap | Close it, or move the question |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Data | Sales by brand by week; which brand streamed when, where, with whom | Dewey's Brand Tracker carries brand-level card spend; read the dataset page for the unit and the years, which is what the map means by a have, and it takes ten minutes; Dewey's Weekly Patterns for store visits | No stream schedule exists anywhere reachable; US card data does not see Taobao or Douyin | Move to US brands whose platform publishes events; then one brand with a public log |
| Comparison | The same brand in weeks it did not stream, or brands that did not stream that week | Both are in the same file | Streaming weeks are chosen weeks and streaming brands are chosen brands, which is another reason those weeks already differed | Line the weeks up around the stream and compare before with after, which meeting 9 names; note it, do not solve it today |
| Skills | A table with one row per brand per week, built in R, Python or Stata | One person on most teams can do it | Thin | Pair that person with a second; meeting 5 drives the file through an AI assistant |
| Time and money | Dewey access, an afternoon to build the table, no money | Dewey is days from registration | Hand-collecting a schedule would be weeks | Not worth it; move the question first |
| Permissions | Dewey's terms of service; nothing human | Covered by the subscription | Scraping a platform's schedule is a terms-of-service question | Meeting 4 teaches it; name it today |
| People and access | Somebody who worked at a brand or agency with a stream log | Team members with e-commerce experience | A log for one brand would close the data row | Ask; people say yes more often than students expect |

The binding row is data. The moves, in order: US brands with announced
events, then one brand with a public log, then collecting it yourself, which
puts the IRB into the permissions row and weeks into the time row, and which
[meeting 8](08-designs-i.qmd) will ask whether you can actually do.

### Case two, the nutrition label

Does a plain-language nutrition label change what shoppers put in the basket?
Shape two, choices people make in a task you set them, half of them shown one
version and half the other. Route two, from a study, here the labelling
literature. This one is nobody's project, on purpose. Value: both, because a
retailer decides whether to relabel its own range and a regulator writing a
labelling rule acts on the same number. Most rooms guess money or skills. The
reveal is that the clock is the row almost nobody would circle.

| Row | Need | Have, and how checked | Gap | Close it, or move the question |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Data | None exists; you build it: two label versions, a basket choice task, and two to four hundred people you pay to take it online | Qualtrics, the survey tool, is free to every Cornell student; nobody on the team holds a Prolific account yet; still pictures of the labels are cheaper and easier to repeat than a live tool | The questionnaire itself does not exist | Nobody teaches this in 6991; draft it in October and bring it to office hours |
| Comparison | Half see the plain-language label, half see the standard one | It is built into the design you would run | None | Meeting 8 asks whether that design is open to you at all |
| Skills | Survey and experiment logic; a difference in means or one regression | No programming needed | The team has not run one | Meeting 8, plus one practice run on classmates that does not count |
| Time and money | Participants at [Prolific's](https://www.prolific.com/pricing) minimum of eight dollars an hour plus the 33 percent academic fee: about five hundred dollars for three hundred people on a ten-minute study, about a thousand at the recommended rate; the IRB puts weeks on the row | No budget | Money, and a clock | A smaller sample buys a coarser answer; and the gate has to start early, which meeting 4 dates |
| Permissions | The IRB, since these are human participants | Nothing yet | Weeks | Meeting 4 says what the gate takes and when it must start |
| People and access | Nobody outside the team | The instructor, if asked | None | Ask in September |

The binding row is time and money, and it is the clock rather than the
dollars. If money is the gap, the sample falls and the answer gets coarser, so
the question narrows to a larger effect, or to showing each person both labels
rather than one. If the clock is the gap, the December proposal carries the
questionnaire and the field date is January, which is what AEM 6992 is for.

### Case three, the flood question, and session B's shared object

Is flood risk priced into house prices, and did a local flood change that?
Every team maps this one, from the same two dataset cards, on the same
template, so the nine maps are comparable and can be corrected against one
another. Shape one, evaluation. Route three, from data, done honestly. It is a
neighbour of Team G and of lead 2 on the
[project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd) page. Value: both, because buyers, FEMA
and flood-insurance pricing act publicly, and insurers, lenders and listing
platforms would pay.

| Row | Need | Have, and how checked | Gap | Close it, or move the question |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Data | Sale prices by parcel with coordinates and dates; a flood-risk measure by ZIP; a list of floods with dates and places | Card 1, Real Estate Transaction Data, says a row is a parcel, a sale, or an assessment, US, 2011 to now, joins on lat/long, ZIP, address; card 2, US Climate Risk, one row per ZIP, five hazard ratings 1 to 100 | The first trap: the risk measure carries no dates, so the before and after has to come from a second source the team does not yet have. The third trap: card 1's unit is not settled, so "sales" is a filter somebody has to write, and a have you have not opened is a need | Free: [OpenFEMA disaster declarations](https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/disaster-declarations-summaries-v2), which are listed by county, so the second trap is matching ZIP codes to counties, with a lookup table that is [free from HUD with a HUD USER account](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps_crosswalk.html) |
| Comparison | ZIPs with the same flood rating that did not flood, before and after the event | Both groups are in card 1 once the event list exists | The flooded ZIPs may have been trending differently already | Meeting 9 turns this into a design and names the assumption carrying it; today it is enough that the comparison exists in the file |
| Skills | Joining two large files on ZIP; a table with one row per parcel per sale | Somebody who has handled millions of rows | Usually nobody | Meeting 5, and a librarian |
| Time and money | Dewey days; no money; the transactions extract is large | Registration may still be pending | Days | Register tonight if not done |
| Permissions | Dewey's terms; no human subjects | Covered | None | Write none on the sheet; a blank row is not the same as none |
| People and access | Nobody in particular | A librarian for the lookup table | None | Fifteen minutes with the business librarian |

Three things about these files are easy to miss, and the draw is where you
find out whether you missed them. A team that writes "have" against card 2
without noticing that it carries no dates loses that row to the first attacker
who names it. Matching ZIP codes to counties is the second. The third is the
cheapest and the best find: card 1 says one row is a parcel, a sale, or an
assessment, so a team that writes "one row per sale" has broken the rule
printed on its own sheet.

All three are resource facts and not findings about the rows. The row-level
interrogation of these files is [meeting 5](05-tools-and-ai.qmd). Today it is
enough to notice that a have you have not opened is a need.

Then the point of the case. When you start from data, nothing looks missing,
so the question is only as good as its buyer. Go back to the question of who
would act differently, and name the insurer, the lender or the assessor who
would act.

### The resource map template

One page, landscape, one per question. The header carries your team letter,
the date, the question in one line, its route, its shape, and one line naming
the role that acts or the firm that pays.

| Row | What the question needs | What we have, and how we checked | Gap | Who closes it, by when, or how the question moves |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Data | Which dataset, who holds it, and what it must contain | Dataset page read, on which date; file opened, or not | | |
| Comparison | Where the counterfactual comes from: which units, which period. Printed beside the row: compared to what? Would those two groups have looked the same anyway? | | | |
| Skills | Language, method, who on the team has run one | | | |
| Time and money | How long: now, days, weeks, months, longer; dollars; the deadline it must meet | | | |
| Permissions | Ethics review by the IRB, a data-use agreement, terms of service, or none, and how long each takes | | | |
| People and access | Who you know who holds the data, the decision, or the site | | | |

Three lines sit under the table, and they are the ones I read first.

- The row that stops you is ____, and it has to close by ____.
- If it does not close, the question becomes ____.
- Decision log, one line per move: what changed, when, why.

Four rules are printed under those lines. A "have" with no "how checked"
counts as a need. A blank permissions row is not the same as "none", so write
none if it is none. "Unknown, X checks by Friday" is an acceptable gap entry.
And the last column is where the plan lives.

The access ladder runs in small type at the foot of the sheet, with the same
seven durations in the same words as the slide and the
[data sources](../data-sources.qmd) page: library databases and the census,
now; the Nielsen public-use extract, now with your netID; Dewey, days; your
own survey or online experiment, weeks, after review by the IRB; full
Kilts-Nielsen data, months; a data-use agreement with a firm, months and it
may fail; confidential microdata via FSRDC, longer than this degree. If the
page and the sheet ever disagree, I edit the page, not the sheet.

The last line on the sheet is the point of the whole exercise. The map is not
filled in once. A resource that turns out missing changes the question, the
changed question changes the rows, and every redraw is the plan doing its
job, not the plan failing.

## Session B · 3:30 to 4:30

A lettered envelope is on your table before session A starts, marked "do not
open until 3:30". It holds everything your team needs this afternoon, plus the
picture you drew last Wednesday of what you would change and what you would
measure. Bring your half sheet back from the first hour, because line two of
it goes straight into the role box on your question sheet.

**Check in first, in writing.** Nine minutes, one sheet per team. Who is
here. What you did since September 2. What is stuck. Who does what next, with
a name and a date on every line. One optional question to me, which I answer
by email before Friday. Your submitter signs it. In week three, "nothing is
stuck yet" is an acceptable answer, and it is the answer I expect from most
tables. The sheet goes in the envelope when the timer stops.

**Then the shared case, and every team maps the same question.** Is flood
risk priced into house prices, and did a local flood change that? Use the two
dataset cards, one on real estate transactions and one on US climate risk, and
one map sheet. The needs column is already printed, so your work is the other
three columns. Write what you have and how you checked it, the gap, and who
closes it. Then fill the three bottom lines: the row that stops you, its date,
and what the question becomes if that row does not close. Fourteen minutes.
Because every team maps the same object, the nine maps are comparable, and
that is the whole reason for a shared case.

**Then one team is drawn at random to read its map aloud.** Two slips come
out of the cup before the writing starts, and the second team is on deck, so
nobody knows in advance whether they are up. The submitter reads from the
sheet at its own table and the room turns. Blanks are read aloud as blanks.
Then the room attacks. An attack names a specific row that is blank,
unchecked or wrong. Calling a map thin is not an attack. A point for every
attack that lands, on the tally sheet at the front. I close with whichever
trap nobody found.

**Then your own project, which is the half you hand in.** Nine minutes for
the question sheet. Three candidate questions, from at least two different
routes if you can manage it. Each one labelled with its route, its shape, and
the role of the person who would act on the answer or pay for it. Run one
candidate through all four filters in writing, not in your heads. Cross a
second one out and name the filter that killed it, because a team that kills
nothing has not used the filter. For the third, write the one row that would
kill it. Then name which candidate gets mapped.

**Then the map, for the survivor only.** Twelve minutes. Every gap gets a
person and a date, or the question moves. "Unknown, with a name and a date"
counts. Fill the three bottom lines, because those are the lines I read
first.

I come round once between the question sheet and the end. It is one question
and one answer per table, not a consultation, so ask me the one that is
actually blocking you.

Four sheets go in your envelope before you leave: the check-in, the shared
map, the question sheet, and your own map. Your submitter brings the envelope
to the front. Your pitch gets built from the question sheet and the map. A
question you kill today is a month you do not lose in March.

## Handouts

[Resource map and question sheet](../handouts/resource-map.qmd). The map
template, one page per question, and the question sheet you fill this
afternoon. It reprints the two dataset cards for the shared case, so the
reading is one page in front of you rather than three pieces of paper.

[Team check-in sheet](../handouts/check-in.qmd). One sheet per team, and you
fill it every week from now on. Who is here, what you did, what is stuck, who
does what next with a name and a date, and one question for me.

[Project teams](../handouts/02-teams.qmd). The nine questions this class is
asking, and who is working on each. Seven of the nine appear on the screen
today, always as the team's own sentence.

## Where to read more

[Adams, Khan, Raeside and White](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) on
the research cycle, and on the literature review and critical reading. That
DOI resolves to the 2007 edition, titled *Research Methods for Graduate
Business and Social Science Students*, so check the chapter numbers against
whichever copy you open.

[Sarasvathy on effectuation](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2001.4378020) is the
theory paper behind "start from your means". Read it for the list of resources
it implies, not for a law about entrepreneurs.

[Arrow, Economic welfare and the allocation of resources for
invention](https://www.nber.org/chapters/c2144) is where public value comes
from. Knowledge is expensive to make and cheap to copy, so whoever makes it
cannot charge the people who benefit.

[McLean and Pontiff](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) is the private-value
paper, and it is the most useful twenty pages in this list if your interest
is finance.

[Sandberg and Alvesson](https://doi.org/10.1177/1350508410372151) separate
looking for a hole in the literature, which they call gap-spotting, from
challenging what the literature takes for granted, which they call
problematization. It is a distinction for people writing for journals rather
than for this course, so read it only if you want the research-side version of
today.
